topics.title: Mathcounts Warm-Up 5
topics.text:
Here are the problems.



1. Fido has to climb five stairs. If he steps on at least three of the five stairs, but never climbs more than three stairs in one step, in how many possible ways can Fido climb the stairs? SolutionHere is my own solution:



We can apply a little casework. Then, the amounts here are small enough that we can simply list out combinations.

Let's call the steps $1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ (ascending from the bottom step). When we list out combinations, the only ones that work are the ones that end in $5$ (since otherwise Fido won't have climbed the whole staircase) and start with $1, 2$ or $3$ (since otherwise he climbs more than three steps on his first step).



Now we split this into cases.

Case A: Fido steps on exactly three steps. Here are the possible combinations. We might be listing these out, but we can at least do it in an organized way!

Starting on step 1:

$1, 2, 5$

$1, 3, 5$

$1, 4, 5$

Starting on step 2:

$2, 3, 5$

$2, 4, 5$

Starting on step 3:

$3, 4, 5$

So Case A gives us $6$ ways.

Case B: Fido steps on exactly four steps. Here are the possible combinations:

Starting on step 1, then step 2:

$1, 2, 3, 5$

$1, 2, 4, 5$

Starting on step 1, then step 3:

$1, 3, 4, 5$

Starting on step 2:

$2, 3, 4, 5$

So Case B gives us $4$ ways.

Case C: Fido steps on all five steps. There is only one possible combination, and it's pretty obvious:

$1, 2, 3, 4, 5$

So Case C gives us $1$ way.



Adding up the results from each case, we get $6 + 4 + 1 = 11$, so our answer is $\boxed{11}$.




2. A school of 100 fish swims in the ocean and comes to a very wide horizontal pipe. The fish have three choices to get to the food on the other side: swim above the pipe, through the pipe or below the pipe. If we do not consider the fish individually, in how many ways can the entire school of fish be partitioned into three groups with each group choosing a different one of the three options and with at least one fish in each group? SolutionNo one has answered this correctly, so here is my own solution:



We have three groups, each taking a different way; Group $A$, Group $B$, Group $C$.



Now we 'stick' one fish in each group, because the problem requires that there be at least one fish in each group. We now have $100 - (1 \cdot 3) = 97$ fish to spread around however we wish. Now, using the stars and bars method, we have $97$ objects, or stars, and $2$ divisions, or bars. This means we have $99$ 'slots' and we are choosing two of them to be bars. So we have $99C2$.



$99C2 = \frac{99\cdot98}{2!} = \frac{99 \cdot 98}{2} = 99 \cdot \frac{98}{2} = 99 \cdot 49 = 4851$.



So our answer is $\boxed{4851}$.




3. The figure shown (see attached image) consists of a regular hexagon and all of its diagonals. How many triangles in the figure have at least two congruent sides?   Solution@alifenix- provided a nice solution in this post. Here it is:



[quote=alifenix-]

We can start with the obvious: the 6 equilateral triangles that have the same side length as the hexagon (6). Also, you can see 2 big equilateral triangles. (8)



Then, we can isolate one of the small equilateral triangles and see how many triangles are in it; 1, since only the one on the top is isoceles. There are six, so we can add 6 to our current total. (14)



If we take two of the adjacent triangles, we can see 3; two (120-30-30) triangles, one going up and one going down, and finally one more that looks equilateral and whose top point is a vertex of the hexagon. 3 times 6 of these make 18. (32)



If we take three of the adjacent triangles (half of the hexagon) then we can find one more, a big 120-30-30 triangle stretching from two opposite vertices, going through the center. 6 x 1 = 6 (38). Therefore, the answer is $ \boxed{38}$.[/quote]

topics.title: A few problems on motion
topics.text:
1. Tag:

In a game of tag, the playing field is a 100 by 100 meter square. The tagger constantly moves towards the non-tagger at a speed of 1 meter per second, and never tires. The non-tagger moves at a speed of 1 meter per second and never tires too. The tagger starts in one corner, and the non-tagger starts in the opposite corner. What do you think the non-tagger should do to ensure survival for as long as possible?



2. Lost in the woods:

Person A and Person B live in a cottage at (0,0). Person B goes to collect firewood, but does not return, so Person A sets out after Person B. They both walk at the same speed, and they will notice each other if they are decently close. What is the best strategy for Person B, so that he gets found? What is the best strategy for Person A, even if Person B does not stick to the optimal strategy (keep in mind Person A does not want to get lost himself)?



3. Dodgeball:

Two people play free for all Dodgeball in a 100 by 100 meter square. They both move at 1 meter per second, and both can throw a dodgeball at 5 meters per second. Each has an unlimited supply of dodgeballs, and they can move anywhere in the square (they don't have to stick to one side). If they start in opposite corners, what is a good strategy? Assume that they can only throw 1 dodgeball per 5 seconds, and dodgeballs can only travel until they hit a wall.

topics.title: 9 Paradox?
topics.text:
I was busy writing problems (like you know how I like writing problems right?)



But then I came across a problem I wrote with two solutions:



Let $S=\{1,2,3,...,2016\}$, and let $A$ be a random subset of $S$. Let $B$ be a random subset of $S$ such that the intersection of $A$ and $B$ is the empty set. Let $C$ and $D$ be random subsets of $A$ and $B$ respectively, and $E$ be the union of $C$ and $D$. What is the expected value of the number of elements of $E$?



Solution 1: Do this one step at a time

Consider the expected value of the number of elements in $A$. Notice that, for every element, they have two choices, be in $A$ and $S$, or be in just $S$. Since $A$ is chosen randomly, these occur with equal probability, so the expected value of the number of elements in $A$ is $\frac{2016}{2}=1008$.



We know $B$ is a random subset of the remaining $1008$ elements. By our previous logic, $B$ has an expected value of $\frac{1008}{2}=504$ elements. We do the same thing with $C$ and $D$, finding expected values of $504$ and $252$ respectively. Thus we add and get the expected value is $756$ elements in $E$.



Solution 2: Do this all at once

Consider this from an element's perspective. It can have the following possibilities:

It is only in $S$

It is only in $A$ and $S$

It is only in $B$ and $S$

It is in $E, C, A$, and $S$

It is in $E, D, B$, and $S$

Of these $5$ choices, only $2$ are in E. Thus the expected value is $(\frac{2}{5})(2016)$, which is $806.4$.



As it is obvious, they cannot both be right, but I cannot find the flaw in either of them...

topics.title: Squeep National Olympics
topics.text:
Feel Free to Post Your Very Own Squeep National Olympics Problems



Post answers to any problems you can do



OPENING CEREMONY

1. For the Opening Ceremony, there will be a fireworks show. There are 12 cannons who are considered equal. There will be fireworks at 4 places: The North Gate, The South Gate, The East Gate, and The West Gate. If the North and South Gates should have twice as as many fireworks as the East and West Gates, how many cannons will be at the North Gate.



2. The Official Squeep Olympics YouTube account posts an official video of the Opening Ceremony, which gets 1024 thousand views. Each video showing the Opening Ceremony afterwards gets half as many views as original, for example, the next video gets 512 thousand views, and the next gets 256 thousand views. Unofficial YouTube accounts keep on posting videos, until they don't get any views at all. What is the total number of views for ALL the Opening Ceremony videos, to the nearest thousand?



3. The Squeep Olympics Team set the ticket price for the Opening Ceremony last year to $100 per Squeep. 50,000 Squeeps attended the Opening Ceremony. The Squeep Olympics Team knows that by every dollar they raise the ticket price by, 1,000 less Squeeps will attend the Opening Ceremony. What should the ticket price be, in whole dollars, so that the maximum profit is gained?



Track & Field



1. The perfectly circular track in which the Squeeps must run around is 10 meters wide, split into ten lanes each 1 meter wide. Squeeps run in the center of their lane, and the innermost Squeep has to run a complete lap around the track. If the race is to be fair, the Squeeps on the outer ring should have a head start, so that the distance the Squeeps have to run is equal. How far of a head start should the Squeep on the outermost lane have on the Squeep on the innermost lane? Express your answer in terms of $\pi$.



2. For the Squeep Shot Put event (using glucks), the representative of Squeepland knows that he can throw the gluck at the speed of 2 meters per second. He also knows, that on the planet Squeeplanet, gravity accelerates objects towards the ground by 40 centimeters per second, every second. (In other words, if he threw the gluck straight up, one second later, it would be moving at 2 meters per second - 40 centimeter per second = 160 centimeters per second in the upwards direction). The Squeep wants to know whether it should throw the Squeep at a 30, 45, or 60 degree angle to the ground to ensure maximum distance?



3. The Track and Field events are as follows: The events on the track are: the 100 meter dashes, the 200 meter dashes, the 400 meter dashes, the 5K, and the 10K. The events on the Field are Shot Put, Javelin Throw, Discus Throw, Gluck Fight, and Pole Vaulting. The track events take, including commercials, 20 minutes, 30 minutes, 40 minutes, 1 hour, and 1 hr 30 mins. The Field events all take 48 minutes. If only one Track, and one Field event can take place at any time, and there are no times where the Track or the Field is empty, then how many ways can the Squeep Olympics Team organize the events so that there will be a period of time where the 10K is being run, and the Gluck Fight is occuring?



4. The Gluck Fight event is like a water balloon fight, but with glucks. There are two squeeps, one at (0,0), and one at (30, 45). They each throw a gluck at each other, the first with speed 3 units per second, and the second with speed 4 units per second. The moment they throw the glucks, a wind blows, causing the glucks to move off course by 2 units per second in the positive y direction. What is the smallest possible distance at any moment between the glucks?



5. According to tradition, Squeeps in 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, and 5th place in a race get the following medals: The Golden Gluck, The Silver Gluck, The Bronze Gluck, The Crystal Gluck, and the Natural Gluck. However, this year, the Crystal Gluck and the Natural Gluck are considered of equal value, so someone in 4th or 5th place would accept either. The Crystal Gluck is considered of equal value to the Silver Gluck and the Bronze Gluck, and the Bronze Gluck is considered of equal value to the Gold Gluck. A Squeep will accept the Gluck he is supposed to get (e.g. 5th place would accept the Natural Gluck), or a Gluck someone who finished before him is supposed to get (e.g. 4th place would accept the Golden Gluck). A Squeep would also accept a Gluck that is DIRECTLY OF EQUAL VALUE to his Gluck (1st would accept Gold or Bronze, but not Crystal, even though Crystal=Bronze). How many ways can the Glucks be handed out?



To be continued...

topics.title: Counting Questions
topics.text:
Solve this problem first:

Given 5 apples, 3 indistinguishable red ones, and 2 indistinguishable green ones, find the number of ways to split them among three indistinguishable wicker baskets.



Now solve this one:

Suppose now, that someone will eat a random apple from one of the baskets. What is the probability that it is a green apple from the middle basket (now the baskets are distinguishable)?



Now solve this one:

The eaten apple was replaced. A golden apple is placed in a random basket. What is the probability that a basket contains 3 apples, but does not contain the golden apple?



Now solve this one:

All the apples were dumped out. There are 10 indistinguishable green apples and 10 indistinguishable red ones to be split among the now distinguishable baskets. If each basket must contain a green apple and a red one, how many ways are there to split the apples?



Now solve this one:

How many ways are there to do the previous problem, if each basket must contain an apple, but not necessarily both a green and red one?



Now solve this one:

The 10 green and red apples are now randomly arranged in a circle. I start eating the apples starting with the first one, and follow the rule:

-If the apple I eat is red, go to the next apple and eat it

-If the apple I eat is green, then go to the next red apple and eat it

What is the expected number of apples I must eat before I eat all the red ones?



Finally, solve this hard one:

4 red and 4 green apples are arranged evenly around a circle, in a random order. All lines between red apples are drawn, and all lines between green apples are drawn. What is the most number of intersections inside the octagon formed by the apple? The least number?

topics.title: Tricky Magic Square Jigsaw Puzzle... (need help)
topics.text:
499th post!

I found this cool puzzle on the Internet: http://www.mathsisfun.com/games/magic-square-game.html. I've actually known this puzzle for a long time. (probably about 2 years) It's where you have 16 puzzle pieces with the numbers 0 to 15 on them, and you have to arrange them so the rows and columns add to 30. But they have certain restrictions, puzzle pieces with spokes sticking out in opposite directions cannot be adjacent so their spokes collide. However, spokes may go outside the grid, and holes in the pieces may be adjacent to each other. I discovered something else, as well. When you look at the left part of a piece, and go counterclockwise, pretending the inward holes are 0, and the outward spokes are 1, you get the number's 4-digit binary form.



The only thing I could determine was that the piece with 0 on it will always be able to be placed after you place the other 15 pieces. Not much else was obvious. Let's work through this puzzle together. If you don't know what we're talking about, click the link at the top of this topic!

topics.title: 9 Read the passage and see what's wrong
topics.text:
Start out with an equation $-1*-1=1*1$

Thus $(-1)^2=1^2$

Since 1 is positive, we can take the square root, so $\sqrt{(-1)^2}=\sqrt{1^2}$

So ${([-1]^2)}^{\frac{1}{2}}={(1^2)}^{\frac{1}{2}}$

So $(-1)^{2*{\frac{1}{2}}}=1^{2*{\frac{1}{2}}}$

Thus $(-1)^1=1^1$

Therefore $-1=1$

topics.title: Sleepless In Seattle
topics.text:
For this problem set, you are only allowed to use the following strategies:



Draw a Diagram (include your diagram/sketch if you use this strategy and make sure you actually use the diagram to help you solve the problem)

Make a Systematic List (be sure your list IS, in fact, systematic!)

Eliminate Possibilities (be sure you explain why certain possibilities are being eliminated!)

Matrix Logic (be sure to actually include the matrix and provide enough details in your explanation for me to follow your logic!

Look for a Pattern (be sure to explain the pattern!)

Guess and Check (be sure you include a chart with your "guestimates" and your checks.)

Identify Subproblems (be sure you make it obvious what your subproblems are!)



"Sleepless in Seattle



I heard an interesting story on the news last night about a guy from Seattle.  In this story, Barry was having a problem with recurring nightmares.  Barry reported that he was having a nightmare every 19 days about 19 ghosts scaring him out of his wits by jumping out of a 1919 Hupmobile and saying “boo” 19 times.  (Don’t ask me to explain this – it’s Barry’s nightmare!)  He was also having a nightmare every 13 days about 13 black cats crossing his path in front of his house, located at 1313 Thirteenth Street.  He had a bad week in April, when on the night of Friday, April 5th, he had the nightmare about the 19 ghosts saying “boo” 19 times.  The very next night, he had the nightmare about the 13 black cats.  Barry knows he can handle these nightmares when they occur from time to time, but lately he’s been really worried that they might both occur on the same night.  Do they ever occur on the same night by the end of the year?  If so, on what date?"
